_comment: Peritonitis with perforated peptic ulcer: the acute abdomen prototype. Almost every bedside finding is an emphasis overlay on shared surgery/core skills; the disease owns the mechanism (one spill, one picture), the three stages, sealed versus free perforation, and source control with Graham patch.
name: Peritonitis and perforated peptic ulcer
fullName: Generalised peritonitis due to perforated peptic ulcer
oneLine: Sudden upper abdominal catastrophe, and the hours that decide survival

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: What secondary peritonitis is, and why the perforated ulcer is its prototype

chapters.title: Approach to the patient
chapters.blurb: Be gentle first: this abdomen punishes rough hands

chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Middle aged men with neglected ulcer pain carry the highest risk

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Perforation of peptic ulcer clusters in middle aged men, often daily wage earners with irregular meals, spicy food, bidi smoking and self taken painkillers. A neglected ulcer past in a low income patient who never sought care for hunger pains is the classic background, so age, occupation, residence and habits carry real diagnostic weight here.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: Sudden, stabbing, and then spreading: the tempo tells the story

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect a sudden stabbing upper abdominal pain, often after a meal, that the patient timestamps to the hour. Ask where it started with one finger, how it spread all over, and whether movement, cough or breathing worsen it.

skill.hx.surg.acute_abdomen.expect: Expect the classic perforation tempo: abrupt epigastric onset, spread across the whole abdomen within hours, pain referred to the right shoulder from diaphragmatic irritation, and later pain in the right iliac fossa as contents track down the right gutter.

skill.hx.surg.chronic_dyspepsia_ulcer.expect: Expect a neglected ulcer past behind the catastrophe: rhythmic hunger pains eased by food or antacids over months, previous vomiting of blood or black stools, and regular painkiller tablets. Its absence does not exclude perforation, since a first ulcer can perforate without warning.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: The ulcer past and the habits that broke it open

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Stillness, fast pulse and dry tongue before the abdomen is touched

skill.gen.surg.survey.expect: Expect a quiet motionless patient lying with hips flexed, with anxious facies and cold sweat in late cases. Stillness is the survey finding here, the opposite of the tossing of colic.

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for dehydration early: sunken eyes, dry tongue, drawn cheeks. Toxaemia shows as a dry brown tongue with a fast pulse, and pallor suggests chronic blood loss from the same ulcer disease.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Expect a pulse that starts normal and quickens as peritonitis spreads, with falling pressure and rising respiratory rate. Temperature is often normal in the first hours, so a normal temperature excludes nothing, but low grade fever with tachycardia can appear within hours as peritonitis spreads, so early fever never excludes perforation either.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.expect: Expect tachycardia, thready pulse, cold periphery and falling urine output as third spacing and sepsis take hold. Waiting for a dramatic pressure drop means waiting for decompensated shock.

chapters.title: Abdominal examination
chapters.blurb: Board like rigidity, lost liver dullness and a silent abdomen

skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.expect: Expect generalised board like rigidity with rebound tenderness everywhere, thoracic breathing with no abdominal movement, and a silent abdomen. Elicit rebound and percussion tenderness gently; rough handling adds nothing and costs the patient's trust.

skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.expect: Expect obliteration of liver dullness on percussion down the right mid axillary line, exquisite tenderness of the pelvic peritoneum on rectal examination, and complete absence of bowel sounds. Together with rigidity this is the bedside diagnosis.

skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.expect: Expect release tenderness in all quadrants rather than one spot. Tenderness that has spread to the left iliac fossa, or to the right fossa from an epigastric start, marks spreading peritonitis and demands immediate surgical review.

skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.expect: Know these signs to avoid the classic trap: tracked gastric contents make the right iliac fossa tender in perforation. The epigastric origin of the pain and generalised rigidity, not a migrating pain with localised fossa signs, separate the two.

skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.expect: Use this examination as the contrast: obstruction is noisy with visible peristalsis and colicky restlessness, while perforation peritonitis is silent with stillness. A silent abdomen with rigidity is never obstruction without strangulation.

stations.title: Examine the acute abdomen
stations.task: This 48 year old man has had sudden severe upper abdominal pain for six hours. Examine his abdomen and present your findings.
examinerQuestions: You found board like rigidity with absent bowel sounds. Why is this peritonitis and not intestinal colic?
Liver dullness is obliterated on percussion. What does this signify, and does its absence exclude perforation?
His pain has eased since arrival but the abdomen is still rigid. Can he be sent home?

stations.title: Take a perforation history and assess risk
stations.task: This 48 year old man has sudden upper abdominal pain. Take a focused history in six minutes and be ready to state what caused it and what happens next.
examinerQuestions: What three facts in his story point to a chronic duodenal ulcer behind this perforation?
His pain started in the epigastrium and is now also in the right iliac fossa. Explain the route.
Name the single investigation you would order first, and what resuscitation starts alongside it.

skill.reasoning.peritonitis.basics.title: What peritonitis from a perforated ulcer is
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.basics.oneLine: A hole in the gut wall turns a contained leak into a whole abdomen emergency
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.basics.why: Peritonitis is not one disease but one response of the peritoneum to very different insults. Knowing which insult you face decides whether the answer is an operation tonight or antibiotics alone, and mixing them up kills.

teach.heading: Secondary peritonitis and its prototype
teach.body:
Secondary peritonitis means infection or chemical irritation of the peritoneal cavity from a leaking viscus. Its commonest surgical prototype in an adult Indian ward is a perforated peptic ulcer, usually anterior duodenal, spilling acidic gastric contents into the free peritoneal cavity.

The leak starts as chemical peritonitis from acid and enzymes, and bacterial infection follows within hours. That two phase course explains why the patient looks shocked before he looks septic, and why early operation matters more than the choice of antibiotic.

teach.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary: three different answers

rows: Resuscitation plus source control, usually operation
Bacterial seeding without a hole, as in cirrhosis with ascites
Persistent infection after treatment, often in intensive care
Support, cultures, search for an undrained focus

teach.heading: Why the duodenum perforates first
teach.body:
Chronic duodenal ulceration erodes the wall from inside until only a thin layer holds. A sudden rise in pressure, straining or a heavy meal, or continued painkiller use, breaks that last layer, and the hole is usually small but the spill is highly irritant.

Posterior ulcers bleed into the pancreas instead of perforating freely, which is why a past of vomiting blood and a present perforation can belong to the same patient with two different ulcers, or even two faces of one disease.

probes.q: What does secondary peritonitis mean, and what is its commonest adult prototype here?
probes.a: Peritoneal contamination from a leaking viscus, most typically a perforated peptic ulcer spilling gastric contents.

probes.q: Why does a perforated ulcer patient look shocked before he looks septic?
probes.a: The first phase is chemical peritonitis from acid and enzymes, and bacterial infection follows hours later.

probes.q: A cirrhotic patient with ascites develops peritonitis with no free gas. Does he need a laparotomy?
probes.a: No. That picture fits primary peritonitis from bacterial seeding, treated with antibiotics and paracentesis, and laparotomy would add harm without a hole to close.

skill.reasoning.peritonitis.signs.title: The perforation picture
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.signs.oneLine: One spill explains the still patient, the board abdomen and the silent gut
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.signs.why: Perforation is the cleanest example in abdominal examination of one mechanism generating a coherent set of signs. Acid on the parietal peritoneum explains the posture, the rigidity, the percussion finding and the silence together, so the signs are read as one picture, not a list.

teach.heading: Stillness, rigidity and silence belong together
teach.body:
The patient lies perfectly still, often with hips flexed, and resists any movement, cough or deep breath, because every jolt drags the inflamed parietal peritoneum. This stillness alone separates peritonitis from colic, where the patient tosses and rolls.

The abdominal wall is rigid like a board from reflex spasm, tender everywhere with rebound, and bowel sounds vanish into a silent abdomen as generalised ileus sets in. One irritant explains all three, which is why finding one should send you hunting for the other two.

teach.heading: Loss of liver dullness means free gas
teach.body:
Gas escaping with the spill rises under the diaphragm and replaces the normal dull note over the liver with resonance when percussed down the right mid axillary line. This is the bedside proof of a perforated hollow viscus.

Absence of the sign does not exclude perforation, since a small leak may release too little gas to detect. But when present with board like rigidity, the diagnosis is made at the bedside, before any film.

teach.heading: The three stages, and the trap in the middle
points: Stage of peritoneal irritation, the first few hours: sudden stabbing upper abdominal pain, stillness, board like rigidity, a pulse that may still be normal but quickens as peritonitis spreads.
Stage of reaction or illusion of recovery: pain eases as exudate dilutes the acid, and the patient feels better while peritonitis spreads.
Stage of diffuse peritonitis: distension, rising pulse, falling pressure, silent abdomen, dehydration and toxaemia.
Never discharge or delay on the second stage. Improvement of pain with a still rigid abdomen is the most dangerous moment in this disease.

probes.q: How does the posture of peritonitis differ from colic at first glance?
probes.a: Peritonitis lies perfectly still and resists movement, while colic tosses, rolls and seeks comfort.

probes.q: Percussion down the right mid axillary line is resonant over the liver area. What does this mean?
probes.a: Free gas under the diaphragm, pneumoperitoneum from a perforated hollow viscus.

probes.q: Pain eases markedly six hours after a sudden onset, but the abdomen stays rigid. What has happened?
probes.a: The stage of reaction: exudate has diluted the acid so pain lessens while peritonitis spreads, and it must never be mistaken for recovery.

skill.reasoning.peritonitis.differential.title: What else looks like a perforation
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.differential.oneLine: Sudden upper abdominal pain has mimics above and below the diaphragm
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.differential.why: Operating for a perforation that is really a heart attack or pancreatitis harms twice: the real disease goes untreated and a laparotomy is added. The differential is worked through before the abdomen is opened, never after.

teach.heading: Below the diaphragm: the surgical mimics
teach.body:
Acute cholecystitis stays under the right ribs with fever and a tender palpable gallbladder, and the rigidity never becomes board like all over. Acute pancreatitis gives agonising upper abdominal pain with vomiting and shock but the abdomen stays relatively soft for the degree of pain.

Acute appendicitis can mimic perforation when gastric contents track down the right gutter to the right iliac fossa, but asking where the pain started exposes the epigastrium as the origin. Ruptured ectopic and leaking aneurysm mimic with collapse and pallor rather than rigidity.

teach.heading: Above the diaphragm and behind it
points: Inferior myocardial infarction refers pain to the epigastrium with sweating and breathlessness; an ECG is mandatory before calling it surgical.
Basal pneumonia and diaphragmatic pleurisy refer pain to the upper abdomen with fever and hurried breathing; the chest must be examined in every acute abdomen.
Ureteric and biliary colic are intermittent and the patient moves, while perforation pain is constant and the patient freezes.
In children consider primary peritonitis and mesenteric adenitis; in young women always consider ectopic gestation and salpingitis.

teach.heading: How to kill a mimic at the bedside
teach.body:
Three questions remove most mimics: where did the pain start, does the patient lie still or toss, and is the rigidity local or board like all over. A soft abdomen despite severe pain points away from perforation.

Two tests finish the job: liver dullness by percussion for free gas, and an ECG plus chest examination for the thoracic mimics. Only then is the diagnosis of perforation secure enough to plan an operation.

probes.q: Name three surgical mimics of perforated peptic ulcer below the diaphragm.
probes.a: Acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute appendicitis with tracked contents in the right iliac fossa.

probes.q: Why is an ECG mandatory in sudden severe epigastric pain?
probes.a: Inferior myocardial infarction refers pain to the epigastrium and operating on it would be catastrophic.

probes.q: Right iliac fossa tenderness appears hours after epigastric pain. Perforation or appendicitis?
probes.a: Perforation until proven otherwise: gastric contents gravitate down the right paracolic gutter, so the origin in the epigastrium is the discriminating fact.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

skill.investigation.peritonitis.workup.title: Confirming perforation without delaying the operation
skill.investigation.peritonitis.workup.oneLine: One erect film proves it, bloods prepare for theatre, and nothing waits for a report
skill.investigation.peritonitis.workup.why: Investigations in suspected perforation serve two jobs: confirm the hole and prepare the patient for operation. Understanding which test does which stops a student waiting for a CT report while a treatable peritonitis spreads.

teach.heading: The film that proves the hole
teach.body:
Erect chest radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm is the confirmatory test, and it is available in most Indian emergency departments day and night. Take it sitting or erect so the gas rises where it can be seen.

Where the film is equivocal, do not insufflate air through the Ryle tube. Keep the patient nil by mouth with the tube on free drainage, resuscitate, and obtain contrast enhanced CT or urgent surgical review. Contrast CT is also used for suspected sealed perforation or for finding an alternative cause.

teach.heading: Bloods that prepare for theatre, not that make the diagnosis
points: Full blood count: leucocytosis supports an acute inflammatory process and anaemia warns of chronic blood loss.
Urea, creatinine and electrolytes: dehydration and third spacing distort them, and the anaesthetist needs them before theatre.
Serum amylase and an ECG: raised amylase favours pancreatitis and an infarct pattern forbids laparotomy, so both exclude mimics.
Blood grouping and cross matching early, since an operation is likely and blood may be needed.

teach.heading: What not to do
teach.body:
Never order a barium study in a suspected acute perforation; contrast in the free peritoneal cavity worsens chemical peritonitis. Never delay resuscitation or surgical review for a scan in a patient with board like rigidity and free gas already shown.

Ultrasound may show free fluid but cannot reliably show the hole, so a negative ultrasound never overrules the clinical picture. Do not perform diagnostic paracentesis when board like rigidity with free gas already confirms perforation, since a tap adds nothing and risks bowel injury. Peritoneal sampling is considered only by the operating surgeon when the diagnosis or source is unclear, and it is never a student bedside procedure.

probes.q: What single investigation confirms a perforated viscus in most emergency departments?
probes.a: Erect chest radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm.

probes.q: Why are serum amylase and an ECG part of the perforation workup?
probes.a: They exclude the two great mimics: pancreatitis and inferior myocardial infarction.

probes.q: The erect film is normal but the abdomen is board like. What next?
probes.a: Do not exclude perforation: a small leak releases too little gas to see. Resuscitate, keep nil by mouth with a Ryle tube, and get a contrast CT or urgent surgical review rather than waiting.

skill.reasoning.peritonitis.diagnosis.title: Naming the diagnosis and grading the risk
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.diagnosis.oneLine: Peritonitis, due to what, for how long, and how sick the patient is with it
skill.reasoning.peritonitis.diagnosis.why: A diagnosis of peritonitis alone decides nothing. The cause, the duration of the leak and the physiologic state of the patient together decide whether this is a straightforward closure or a damage control case, and that grading happens at the bedside, not in theatre.

teach.heading: A complete diagnostic statement
teach.body:
Name the syndrome, the cause, the duration and the state: generalised peritonitis due to perforated anterior duodenal ulcer of about eight hours with early septic physiology. Each clause carries a decision.

Duration matters because a leak beyond a day brings established sepsis, oedematous tissues and a far sicker patient. State the hours since the sudden onset explicitly, since vague phrases like late presentation hide the single most prognostic fact.

teach.heading: Grading how sick: shock, response and the triad
teach.body:
Grade the physiology: pulse, pressure, urine output and mental state, and whether they improve with fluids. Shock on arrival, little urine, and no response to a fluid challenge mark the high risk patient.

Watch for the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, since its presence turns a definitive repair into a damage control case. Rising intra abdominal pressure with failing organs means compartment syndrome, which needs decompression, not more fluid.

teach.heading: When the hole may have sealed
points: A few perforations seal spontaneously with omentum: pain settles, rigidity localises, the patient improves and contrast study shows no ongoing leak.
Sealed perforation is managed conservatively with close observation, nil by mouth, antibiotics and later ulcer treatment.
The decision to watch is made by a senior surgeon with facilities for immediate operation if the patient worsens.
Any deterioration, spreading tenderness, rising pulse or increasing distension, ends the trial and the patient goes to theatre.

probes.q: What four clauses belong in a complete perforation diagnosis?
probes.a: The syndrome, the cause, the duration in hours, and the physiologic state of the patient.

probes.q: What is the lethal triad and what does it change?
probes.a: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy; it changes a definitive repair into an abbreviated damage control operation.

probes.q: When is it acceptable not to operate a proven perforation?
probes.a: When it has sealed: improving patient, localising signs, no ongoing leak on contrast study, under senior observation with theatre ready.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

skill.annex.peritonitis.stages.title: Stages of perforation and pressure thresholds
skill.annex.peritonitis.stages.oneLine: Three clinical stages and two pressure numbers for the ward and the viva
skill.annex.peritonitis.stages.why: Two small tables carry the facts examiners ask for most: the stage the patient is in, and the pressure at which the abdomen itself becomes the disease. Kept in one place, they are recalled in seconds at the bedside.

teach.heading: The three stages of a perforation

rows: Sudden stabbing pain, stillness, board rigidity, normal pulse
Pain eases, patient feels better, rigidity persists
Silent abdomen with fast pulse and low pressure as spread evolves; distension appears late

teach.heading: Pressure thresholds that change management
teach.body:
Intra abdominal hypertension is a sustained pressure of 12 mmHg or more, measured through the bladder catheter. Abdominal compartment syndrome is pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ failure, and it needs urgent decompression.

These numbers come from critical care measurement, not from bedside guessing. Suspect them when a distended abdomen accompanies falling urine output, rising ventilatory pressure and a tense belly after resuscitation.

probes.q: What are the three clinical stages of a perforation?
probes.a: Irritation, reaction with illusory improvement, then diffuse peritonitis.

probes.q: At what pressures do hypertension and compartment syndrome begin?
probes.a: Sustained 12 mmHg or more is intra abdominal hypertension; above 20 mmHg with organ failure is compartment syndrome.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.treatment.peritonitis.management.title: Managing perforation peritonitis
skill.treatment.peritonitis.management.oneLine: Resuscitate, decompress, cover with antibiotics, close the hole, and watch the belly
skill.treatment.peritonitis.management.why: Perforation kills through shock and spreading infection, not through the hole itself. The hole is closed in minutes in theatre, but the patient is saved in the hours before and after by fluids, decompression, antibiotics and monitoring, and getting that order wrong wastes the operation.

teach.heading: Resuscitation first, alongside diagnosis
teach.body:
Start large bore intravenous fluids at once for the tachycardia, low pressure and poor urine output of third spacing and developing shock. Keep the patient nil by mouth and pass a Ryle tube on free drainage to decompress the stomach and reduce further spill.

Give broad spectrum antibiotics early by the institutional protocol to cover gut organisms, and place a urinary catheter to measure output hourly. Correct physiology before theatre: warm the patient, correct fluids and electrolytes, and arrange blood, since a cold acidotic coagulopathic patient tolerates operation badly.

teach.heading: The operation: wash out and patch the hole
teach.body:
The standard emergency operation is laparotomy with peritoneal washout and omental patch closure of the perforation, the Graham patch, which plugs the hole with living omentum rather than pulling friable edges together.

Where the patient carries the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, abbreviate to damage control: control the leak and contamination quickly, leave the abdomen open under temporary negative pressure closure, restore physiology in intensive care, and return for definitive closure later.

teach.heading: After theatre and the Indian ward reality
points: Continue fluids, antibiotics, stomach decompression and hourly urine measurement until bowel function returns.
Watch bladder pressure where the belly stays tense with falling urine and difficult ventilation, since compartment syndrome needs relook, not more fluid.
Start ulcer healing treatment and test for H pylori after recovery, with counselling to stop painkillers, bidis and alcohol.

At a centre without surgical facility, resuscitate, pass the Ryle tube, start antibiotics and refer urgently to a hospital with theatre; emergency laparotomy care is covered under government schemes such as Ayushman Bharat for eligible families.

probes.q: What are the first four steps on suspecting perforation, before theatre?
probes.a: Intravenous fluids, nil by mouth with Ryle tube decompression, broad spectrum antibiotics, and a urinary catheter for hourly output.

probes.q: What is the standard emergency operation for a perforated duodenal ulcer?
probes.a: Laparotomy with peritoneal washout and Graham omental patch closure of the perforation.

probes.q: When should the surgeon abbreviate to damage control instead of definitive repair?
probes.a: In the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy: control contamination fast, temporary abdominal closure, restore physiology, then return.

cases.title: A mason with a sudden stabbing pain after lunch
cases.opening: Suresh Pal, 48, a mason, was carried into the casualty by his brother. He lies perfectly still on the stretcher, knees drawn up, and whispers that any movement makes the pain worse. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I cannot say much, doctor, the pain is too much. Please ask slowly.

patient.name: Suresh Pal
patient.occupation: Daily wage mason at building sites
patient.residence: A rented room near the site with his brother, family in the village

presenting.reply: Doctor, after lunch today I got a sudden stabbing pain high up in the belly. It was so sharp I had to sit down at once, and now it has spread all over.

cues: what were you doing when it started
onset_tempo.reply: It started all of a sudden, about six hours ago, just after I finished lunch at the site. There was no warning, one moment I was fine and the next I was doubled up.

cues: show me with one finger where it started
where did the pain start first
pain_epigastric_site.reply: It started here, high up in the middle just below the ribs. Now the whole belly hurts, but this is where it began. I can still point to that first spot.

cues: pain in the right lower side now
pain_shoulder_spread.reply: Yes, there is a pain up in my right shoulder too. And a few hours back a new pain started low down on the right side of the belly, though the upper pain came first.

cues: does lying still help the pain
does coughing or breathing deepen the pain
pain_stillness_relief.reply: Lying perfectly still is the only relief. If I move, cough or take a deep breath it becomes much worse. Pressing the belly is unbearable.

vomiting_regurgitation.reply: I vomited once, a small mouthful soon after the pain started. Since then only nausea, no repeated vomiting.

cues: have you passed gas since the pain
absolute constipation of stool and wind
bowel_flatus_stop.reply: No motion and no gas have passed since the pain began six hours ago. Before today my bowels were regular.

fever_course.reply: No fever before today. I feel hot and sweaty now but there was no fever in the days before this pain.

cues: hunger pain in the past months
episodes of upper belly pain before
ulcer_hunger_past.reply: For the last two years I get a burning hunger pain high up that wakes me at night. Eating food or a soda tablet from the chemist settles it. It comes in episodes lasting some weeks.

cues: tablets taken for joint or back pain
how often do you take painkillers
tablets taken on an empty stomach
nsaid_painkiller_use.reply: For my backache from lifting bricks I take painkiller tablets almost daily, bought from the chemist, usually without eating first. Nobody told me they harm the stomach.

tobacco_smoking_drink.reply: I smoke about ten bidis a day for fifteen years. I drink country liquor two or three times a week. Meals at the site are irregular, often very spicy.

cues: black tarry stools in the past
bleed_melaena_past.reply: One year ago I vomited blood once and passed black stools for two days. A doctor gave tablets for ulcer but I stopped them once the pain settled.

comorbidity_sugar_pressure.reply: No diabetes, no pressure problem, no heart trouble that I know. I have never been admitted to hospital before.

previous_operation_scar.reply: No operation ever. This is my first time in a big hospital.

current_medication_today.reply: Only the painkiller tablets for my back and the soda tablets for the hunger pain. Today after the pain started I took nothing.

meals_appetite_loss.reply: My appetite was normal till today and my clothes fit the same. No weight loss, no vomiting after meals before this.

family_home_support.reply: My brother lives with me here. My wife and two children are in the village. My brother will stay with me in hospital.

skill.gen.surg.survey.finding: Lies motionless and supine with hips flexed, resists any movement or cough. Anxious facies with cold sweat on the forehead.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Dehydrated look with sunken eyes and dry coated tongue. No pallor of note, no jaundice.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 118 per minute, thready. Blood pressure 100/64. Respiratory rate 28, thoracic. Temperature 38.4 C. SpO2 94 percent on air.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.finding: Tachycardia with narrow pulse pressure, cool hands and feet, delayed capillary refill. Urine output scanty since catheterisation.

skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.finding: Abdomen flat with no respiratory movement. Board like rigidity in all quadrants with generalised rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds absent on two minutes of auscultation.

skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.finding: Liver dullness obliterated: resonance on percussion down the right mid axillary line. Rectal examination shows exquisite tenderness anteriorly in the rectovesical pouch.

skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.finding: Release tenderness present in every quadrant, maximal in the epigastrium. Tenderness has spread to the right iliac fossa though the pain began above.

skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.finding: No distension yet, no visible peristalsis, no hernial swelling at any orifice. Abdomen silent rather than noisy.

skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.finding: No localised McBurney point rigidity; the whole wall is rigid rather than one spot. Pain began in the epigastrium, not around the umbilicus.

erect_cxr.label: Erect chest radiograph
erect_cxr.result: Free gas under the right diaphragm with a clear crescent. Lung fields normal, no infiltrate. Heart size normal.
erect_cxr.note: This is the confirmatory test: free gas with this story means a perforated viscus until proven otherwise.

blood_counts.label: Full blood count
blood_counts.result: Haemoglobin 12.8 g/dL. Total leucocyte count 14,200 per mm3 with neutrophilia.
blood_counts.note: Leucocytosis fits an acute peritoneal insult; the haemoglobin shows no major chronic blood loss today.

renal_function.label: Urea, creatinine and electrolytes
renal_function.result: Urea 52 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L.
renal_function.note: Needed for resuscitation and for theatre: third spacing and vomiting distort these fast, and the anaesthetist will ask for them.

serum_amylase.label: Serum amylase
serum_amylase.result: Mildly raised at twice the upper limit, far below the range of acute pancreatitis.
serum_amylase.note: Sent to exclude pancreatitis, the great soft abdomen mimic. A modest rise occurs in perforation itself and must not mislead.

ecg_heart.label: Electrocardiogram
ecg_heart.result: Sinus tachycardia at 118. No ST change, no infarct pattern.
ecg_heart.note: Mandatory before calling epigastric pain surgical: an inferior infarct would forbid laparotomy.

usg_abdomen.label: Bedside abdominal ultrasound
usg_abdomen.result: Moderate free fluid with internal echoes in the hepatorenal pouch. No gallbladder wall thickening, no stone seen.
usg_abdomen.note: Free fluid supports peritonitis but never shows the hole; a normal scan would not overrule this clinical picture.

barium_study.label: Barium meal study
barium_study.note: Absolutely contraindicated with suspected acute perforation: barium in the free peritoneal cavity worsens chemical peritonitis.

differentialModel.answer: Generalised peritonitis due to perforated peptic ulcer. Consider acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, acute appendicitis with tracked contents, intestinal obstruction, and basal pneumonia or myocardial infarction as mimics.

diagnosis.answer: Generalised peritonitis due to perforated anterior duodenal ulcer, about six hours old, with early hypovolaemic and septic physiology.

managementModel.answer: Upright resuscitation with intravenous fluids, nil by mouth with Ryle tube drainage, broad spectrum antibiotics, hourly urine monitoring, erect film already done, and urgent laparotomy with washout and Graham omental patch closure.

teachingPoints: The tempo makes the diagnosis before any test: sudden stabbing epigastric pain timestamped to the hour, in a man with a two year ulcer past, is perforation until proven otherwise.
Stillness is the first sign. He lies motionless with flexed hips while colic tosses; that contrast should be read from the doorway.
Right iliac fossa pain arriving hours after an epigastric start is tracked gastric content down the right gutter, not appendicitis. The origin, not the latest site, names the disease.
Loss of liver dullness with board like rigidity is bedside proof of free gas. Its absence would not exclude perforation, but its presence here ends the debate.
Easing pain with a still rigid abdomen is the stage of reaction, not recovery. The patient feels better while peritonitis spreads.
The ECG and amylase are not extras: they exclude the two mimics that forbid or redirect surgery, infarction and pancreatitis.
Barium is forbidden in suspected perforation, and no scan waits out resuscitation. Fluids, Ryle tube, antibiotics and urine monitoring start alongside diagnosis, not after it.
